text: The study “Do the anatomical and physiological properties of a muscle determine its adaptive response to different loading protocols?” examined this exact topic. In the study, young untrained men trained calves in 4 sets of 6–10 or 20–30 repetitions. There was no difference in calf muscle thickness between the groups. This study is one of 23 studies that explored the effects of different loads (and therefore rep ranges) on site-specific muscular hypertrophy that were examined in the influential review paper “Loading Recommendations for Muscle Strength, Hypertrophy, and Local Endurance: A Re-Examination of the Repetition Continuum”. This paper concluded that there is no ideal number of repetitions for hypertrophy in general. To quote directly from the “Conclusions” section, With respect to hypertrophy, the compelling body of literature indicates that similar whole muscle growth (i.e., muscle thickness, CSA) can be achieved across a wide spectrum of loading ranges. The researchers recommend moderate loads (and number of repetitions) from a practical standpoint.

text: Nah, they're two different things. Soreness is mostly just your body reacting to something new, especially the lowering part of lifts. It usually peaks a day or two after and then fades, and after a few weeks of the same workouts you barely get sore at all anymore. That's the repeated bout effect. The muscle is still growing. It just stops complaining. Actual recovery, your muscles being ready to produce force again, usually happens way before the soreness goes away. For normal gym work it's typically within a day or two. So here's the practical test. If you can hit your planned weights and your form feels solid, you're good to train even if you're still a little sore. Chasing zero soreness before every session will just have you waiting around for no reason. And the flip side is true too. No soreness doesn't automatically mean you're recovered. You can run yourself into the ground with zero soreness, especially on frequent heavy training. The thing to actually watch is your performance. If your numbers keep dropping session to session, that's the real signal to back off or take a rest day. Short version: don't schedule your workouts by soreness. Schedule them by how the bar moves.
label: evidence

text: If you minimize saturated fat intake, you’ve already solved the problem. It’s pretty well documented that replacing saturated fats in the diet with unsaturated sources is a reliable way to reduce LDL and mitigate cardiovascular event risk. See the AHA Presidential Advisory on Dietary Fats and CVD: Multiple randomized clinical trials, meta-analyses, prospective observational studies, and animal studies all support the concept of replacement of dietary saturated fats with unsaturated fats to reduce cardiovascular disease. Reducing dietary saturated fat and replacing it with polyunsaturated vegetable oil reduced cardiovascular disease by around 30%, similar to results from statin therapy. Prospective observational studies showed that reducing saturated fat and replacing it with polyunsaturated or monounsaturated fat caused 25% and 15% reductions in coronary heart disease (CHD), respectively. Mortality overall and from other causes was also reduced. Exercise is good and has lots of cardiovascular and other general health benefits. But if you’ve already minimized your saturated fat intake and replaced it with unsaturated sources, you’ve already solved the cholesterol problem and I would expect further improvements in LDL from exercise to be pretty modest. But still, you should exercise anyway, as there are numerous other health benefits and non-lipid risk factors that exercise can impact.

text: I am a College T&F/XC Coach, and a runner myself for 16+ years. A classic workout that many milers like yourself will end up doing in their career is a classic workout that the famous Roger Bannister (1st sub-4:00 miler) would run, and it is perfectly scalable for all milers at all levels of fitness. Here's the workout. 10x400m on a 3-minute clock. That's it. Regardless of splits, you start a 400m interval at the top of every 3 minutes for 10 repeats. If you go faster, you get more rest, and slower, then you get less rest. This is what we call an Indicator Workout, meaning that whatever you can average for this workout per 400m is what you should be able to run 4 times in a row with zero rest. Here's the goal you should shoot for if you want to break 5:00 in the mile. 10x400m @1:15 per 400m on a 3-minute clock. If you accomplish this workout at the specified time, then you'll know you've got the fitness to run the time you want. Roger Bannister did this workout and averaged around 59 seconds before he ran sub-4. This has accurately predicted both my own mile times and the mile times of the athletes I've coached, almost to the millisecond. As you get faster, you can return to this workout and shoot for something quicker, like 1:10 (4:40 mile pace) and 1:05 (4:20 pace).

text: Pull-ups and lat pull-downs differ significantly in mechanics and muscle recruitment patterns. In pull-ups, the entire body is engaged as a single unit. Your core, shoulders, back muscles, and even legs work together to stabilize the movement. This additional engagement increases overall muscle recruitment. Studies also show that Closed Kinetic Chain exercises like the pull-up (where one extremity of the body is fixed while the rest of the body moves) lead to higher motor unit recruitment compared to Open Kinetic Chain movements (such as lat pull-downs), resulting in more efficient muscle contraction. In some machines the pulley ratio could also introduce mechanical friction. It seems on the machines with 1:1 ratio (only 1 pulley, so the weight on the stack is close to "true" weight) friction is almost negligible but it can be more noticeable on machines with more pulleys.
